# Features

The robjc package is a framework built on `R6`, a reference based object-oriented system for R.
Its main features are:

- **Collection classes:** Array, Set, and Dictionary each have mutable and immutable variants.
Use `copy()` and `mutableCopy()` to move between them.
- **Customizable equality:** Compare robjc objects with `isEqual()`.
Implement this method to define what equality means for your class.
- **Object archiving:** Save an object graph and restore its reference relationships.
Classes can also be mapped to different classes when an archive is decoded.

# Creating a class

Use one of four factory APIs to create a robjc class generator.
You can also use `R6Class()` directly, but the factory APIs cover most class definitions.

- `RSObjectClass()` creates a subclass of `RSObject`.
This is the most commonly used factory; its parent class must not be a singleton.
- `RSSingletonClass()` creates a singleton class.
Access its shared instance through `Class$instance`. `Class$new()` always returns that instance.
- `RSScalarClass()` creates a custom wrapper for an R value, such as a logical, numeric, character, factor, or complex value.
Use it when the standard scalar wrappers do not express the distinction your class needs.
- `RSProtocolClass()` creates a subclass of `RSProtocol`.
Protocol classes cannot be instantiated.

Here is a custom class.
The first argument is its name as a character string, and `super_class` specifies its parent.
Instance variables and methods are inherited from the parent, as in other object-oriented systems.
See the [class factory guide](guide_05_ClassFactory.Rmd) for details.

```{r}
library(robjc)

CustomClass <- RSObjectClass(
  "CustomClass",
  super_class = RSObject,
  private = list(var = NULL),
  public = list(
    initialize = function(var) {
      super$initialize()
      if (!is.character(var)) return(NULL)
      self$setVar(var)
      return(self)
    },
    getVar = function() private$var,
    setVar = function(var) private$var <- var
  )
)
```

## Creating and initializing an instance

Call `new(...)` to create an instance.
It allocates the instance, calls `initialize(...)`, and returns **the value returned by `initialize(...)`**.
The initializer sets up instance variables and any other instance state.

Always call `super$initialize()` in your initializer so the parent class can initialize its state.
Return `self` when initialization succeeds.
On failure, you can return another value, such as `NULL`.

```{r}
object <- CustomClass$new("foo")
if (!is.null(object)) print(object$getVar())
failure <- CustomClass$new(1L)
stopifnot(is.null(failure))
```

## Instance variables and methods

Every robjc instance has the basic methods supplied by `RSObject`.
Some of them are listed below; see the [classes and objects guide](guide_02_Classes_Objects.Rmd) for more.

- `class()` returns the instance's class generator.
- `superClass()` returns the parent generator of the instance's class.
- `isKindOf(Class)` checks whether the instance belongs to `Class` or one of its subclasses.
- `isMemberOf(Class)` checks whether the instance belongs directly to `Class`.

## Inspecting an instance

You can inspect an object's class and inheritance.
`class()` and `superClass()` return class generator objects, rather than class names.
`isMemberOf()` checks the direct class; `isKindOf()` includes its ancestors.

```{r}
number <- RSNumber$new(42L)
stopifnot(identical(number$class(), RSNumber))
stopifnot(number$isMemberOf(RSNumber))
stopifnot(number$isKindOf(RSScalar))
stopifnot(identical(number$value(), 42L))
```

# Collections

robjc has three collection families: Array, Set, and Dictionary.
Each family has mutable and immutable classes.
Collections hold robjc objects, so wrap ordinary R values such as integers and character strings in `RSScalar` objects before inserting them.

## Wrapping R values

`RSNumber` and `RSString` are scalar classes that hold R values of length one.
When you know the type, call the corresponding class's `$new()`.
`RSScalar_withValue()` selects a suitable wrapper based on the input value.

```{r}
label <- RSScalar_withValue("Apple")
quantity <- RSNumber$new(3L)
stopifnot(label$isKindOf(RSString))
stopifnot(identical(label$value(), "Apple"))
stopifnot(identical(quantity$value(), 3L))
```

Each scalar class provides a shared NA instance for missing values.
Use `RSNull$null` to represent R's `NULL` as an object.

```{r}
stopifnot(identical(RSNumber$new(NA_integer_), RSNumber$na))
stopifnot(identical(RSScalar_withValue(NULL), RSNull$null))
```

## Using collections

An Array stores values in order, a Dictionary associates values with keys, and a Set stores unique values.
Mutable collection class names contain `Mutable`: for example, `RSMutableArray` is the mutable counterpart of `RSArray`.
Mutable collections let you add and remove elements; immutable collections do not.

Call `copy()` to create an immutable collection from a mutable one.
Call `mutableCopy()` to create a mutable collection from an immutable one.

```{r}
items <- RSMutableArray$new()
items$addObject(label)
items$addObject(quantity)
stopifnot(items$count() == 2L)
stopifnot(identical(items$objectAtIndex(1L), label))

saved_items <- items$copy()  # RSArray
stopifnot(saved_items$isEqual(items))

items$addObject(RSString$new("adding item"))
stopifnot(saved_items$count() == 2L)
```

Dictionary keys and values, and Set elements, must also be robjc objects.
Dictionary and Set use `hash()` and `isEqual()` to find objects.

```{r}
lookup <- RSMutableDictionary$new()
lookup$setObjectForKey(quantity, RSString$new("quantity"))
stopifnot(identical(lookup$objectForKey(RSString$new("quantity"))$value(), 3L))

unique_items <- RSMutableSet$new()
unique_items$addObject(RSString$new("A"))
unique_items$addObject(RSString$new("A"))
stopifnot(unique_items$count() == 1L)
```

When using a custom class as a Dictionary key or Set element, make equal objects return `TRUE` from `isEqual()` and the same value from `hash()`.
Pass the calculated hash through `robjc_normalize_hash()` before returning it so the result is never a missing integer.

To store a null value in a collection, insert `RSNull$null` explicitly.
Collections do not automatically wrap R's `NULL`.

## Saving and restoring objects

`RSKeyedArchiver` creates an archive as an ordinary R list, including the reference relationships among objects.
You can save that list as an RDS file. `RSKeyedUnarchiver$new()` loads the archive; `decode()` restores its objects.

```{r}
shared <- RSString$new("shared value")
archive <- RSKeyedArchiver$new()$archive(list(shared, shared))
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(archive, path)

decoder <- RSKeyedUnarchiver$new(readRDS(path))
decoder$showAllClasses()  # Inspect classes that need manual resolution.
restored <- decoder$decode()
unlink(path)

stopifnot(identical(restored[[1L]], restored[[2L]]))
stopifnot(identical(restored[[1L]]$value(), "shared value"))
```

This example uses only standard robjc classes, so no class mapping is needed.
To restore custom classes, inspect unresolved classes with `showAllClasses()`, assign their target classes with `setClasses()`, and then call `decode()`.
See the [archiving guide](guide_10_Archiving.Rmd) for the full procedure.
